extracted.intended_audience: policy analysts, public finance researchers, economists and commission members analyzing federal-provincial fiscal redistribution in Canada (especially Quebec)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and standards for measuring and comparing federal revenues and expenditures by province (1961–1988), including adjustments to provincial economic accounts, classification of transfer programs, and ways to compute per-capita fiscal gains/losses in constant dollars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustments to provincial economic accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a set of adjustments to Statistics Canada provincial economic accounts to better capture the true interregional redistributive effect of federal operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of such adjustments used in the analysis include: a reallocation of indirect federal taxes on the basis of household consumption; elimination (exclusion) of federal investment income and expenditures for public debt service; write-offs of revenue/expenditure items related to national energy policy; and an adjustment of transfers to governments to include fiscal transfers. These adjustments are intended to better reflect the redistributive content of federal budgetary operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure fiscal redistribution using corrected revenue–expenditure balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the gap between corrected federal revenues and corrected federal expenditures in each region (the 'solde budgétaire fédéral corrigé') as the basis for judging interregional redistribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corrected balance is meaningful both in national surplus and deficit situations and avoids arbitrarily assigning past deficits to particular regions. It can be expressed per capita to allow regional comparisons and historical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express results per capita in constant dollars (1988 base used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present fiscal balances and transfers on a per-capita basis and convert monetary values into constant dollars (1988 used in this study) for historical comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing data to per-capita constant-dollar terms allows clearer interpretation of trends over time and interprovincial comparisons; the report specifically uses 1988 dollars for its series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reallocation of indirect federal taxes by household consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute indirect federal tax receipts across provinces according to household consumption patterns to better locate where tax burdens fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reallocation is used by some studies (and in the Commission's adjustments) so that indirect federal taxes are assigned by consumption rather than where revenue is recorded, improving the geographic accuracy of revenue attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude government investment income and public debt service when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove federal investment income and the service of the public debt from the set of federal expenditures used to measure redistributive operations, where justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several studies differ on this choice. Excluding debt service (on the grounds it is not a direct public service) can materially change provincial balances; the Fraser Institute, for example, excluded debt service in one variant. Explicitly state and justify whether debt service is included or excluded, because results are sensitive to that treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat fiscal transfers (tax points) separately from financial transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish transfers delivered as tax points (transferts fiscaux) from direct cash/financial transfers (transferts financiers) when decomposing total federal transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report decomposes FPE and other transfers into 'transfert fiscal' (e.g., tax points, Quebec's abatement) and 'transfert financier' to show differing province choices and the implications for measured financial flows. Example: Quebec historically received a larger share as tax points (total abatement ~16.5%), reducing the measured financial transfer share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of transfer programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify federal transfers into four categories: Financing of Established Programs (FPE), the equalization (péréquation) program, the Canada Assistance Plan / public assistance regime (RAPC), and 'other programs' (various bilateral federal–provincial agreements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to break down amounts and to analyze which programs drive interregional redistribution and how cuts/policy changes affect different provinces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute FPE contribution using a base indexed factor and then remove fiscal transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate the federal contribution to the Financing of Established Programs by starting from a historical base annual amount indexed (e.g., indexed to GNP factors) and multiplying by provincial population, then subtract fiscal-transfer components (tax points, abatements, equalization-afferent) to obtain the net financial transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report gives an example for Quebec (base amount indexed and then fiscal transfers like 13.5 pp on personal federal tax, corporate tax points, special abatement) and shows how indexation rules changed over time—explicitly document the indexation factor used and any retroactive adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate federal deficits across provinces pro rata to revenue (option used by some studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating a federal deficit as a financial charge, distribute that deficit across provinces in proportion to each province's share of federal revenue to compute a province's net fiscal benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One study method treats the yearly federal deficit as a charge and allocates it by revenue share; others may apportion differently. Clearly state the chosen allocation rule because it affects the computed 'benefit fiscal' of each province.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure regional fiscal gain as excess of expenditures over revenues (per capita) relative to national average
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a region's fiscal gain as the per-capita excess of federal expenditures over federal revenues realized in that region; compare that gain to the national average to determine if a region is a net beneficiary or contributor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regions with a fiscal gain above the national average are net beneficiaries of redistribution. This approach works both in national surplus and deficit years and avoids arbitrarily assigning cumulative past deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about years covered and data limitations (periodization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit analysis to years for which relevant data are available and make periodization choices explicit (e.g., 1961–1988 in this report; some external studies cover only 1970 and 1988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different time coverage can change historical interpretation; explicitly state why a period ends (e.g., preliminary data for 1989 not fully published) and how that affects conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and justify alternative adjustment choices and present sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because different studies apply different adjustments to the provincial accounts, document each choice and, where possible, present results under alternative assumptions to show sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report emphasizes that study-to-study differences arise from diverse adjustments (service of debt inclusion/exclusion, tax reallocations, deficit allocation). To allow comparison, either apply a common set of adjustments or report multiple variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: accounts do not capture non-budgetary federal activities or economic incidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that provincial economic accounts only record the geographic location of federal revenues and budgetary expenditures and therefore cannot capture the full regional impacts of crown corporations, loan guarantees, regulatory policy, trade or transport regulation, or the broader economic incidence of spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state these limits and caution against using the accounts as a complete measure of the regional economic impact of federal policies or as a precise basis for estimating the fiscal consequences of sovereignty (which would require identifying which expenditures a new government would assume).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use provincial accounts alone to estimate sovereignty costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat provincial economic accounts as sufficient to estimate the costs to a province (e.g., Quebec) of assuming all federal budgetary activities in the case of independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accounts assign expenditures to the province where they are paid (e.g., salaries), which may diverge from the additional obligations a sovereign province would face; debt service attribution depends on the share of net federal debt allocated, not simply debt held by residents. Any sovereignty costing requires separate assumptions about which functions would be assumed and how debt would be apportioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret transfer cuts in relation to indexation and program rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing the impact of federal cuts (for example to FPE), evaluate how changes in indexation rules and the growth rate of the total contribution interact with the growth of fiscal transfers to project future financial-transfer outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes that reduced growth of total FPE contributions combined with continuing growth of fiscal transfers (tax points) can lead to declining or zero net financial transfers for provinces—so compute projected trajectories given indexation rule changes.
